en: I shall drive my caravan from Kerüü;
Unless I die, I shall take my revenge
Upon the Kalcha khan of the monks!
Because the Chinese took the horses,
Should we seethe in anguish?!
Does a warrior not encounter hardship?
You are children of a dark day;
Does grief not divide one's reason?!
Does a brave man who rides on patrol
Not encounter every kind of peril?!
Can grief serve as payment?
Because the Kalmak took the horses,
Should we go on grieving?!”
He spoke words of courage to the boys.
The dear hero stood towering;
The dear warrior did not stir at all.
Standing erect, he paid it no heed,
And counted the boys' grief
As less than the hem of his robe.
He fastened on his golden belt-pouch,
And radiance like moonlight touched the face
Of the gray wolf, pure-born from his father.
Your gray wolf grew wrathful,
Standing tall without distress;
He mounted Buurul and rode out,
Your dear prince looming high.
In the broad valley of Üch-Karkyra,
Unable to find the trail here,
He now turned back.
Straight across Charyn and Chara,
Your gray wolf descended
Into the Lower Charyn plain.
Nothing caught his eye;
Where the powerful weather-worker Muradyl
Had driven them away
Could not then be determined.
He searched along the mountainside;
They say he examined in turn
Ylailuu-Kyr and Aigai-Tash,
But found no trail.
He searched Kyygach-Kyr,
And followed the winding Kara-Suu
Along its course.
Unable to find the trail here,
He searched across a great distance.
They say he crossed Üch-Kaiky,
And passed through Ükürchü;
He searched down through Üch-Kapkak,
Along the flowing waters
Of the Tekes River.
No trail appeared to his eyes;
Where the mighty weather-worker Muradyl
Had driven them,
And which way he had gone, remained unknown.
The earth billowed into dust,
And Semetey's head reeled.
Through rugged ground and a great valley,
He searched up the great valley;
Your gray wolf, touched by Khizr,
Searched across a great distance.
At Kara-Bulak and Moinok-Tash,
He now turned back.
Turning back and making ready,
Receiving wisdom from the unseen,
The lion son of the bloodthirsty hero
Now went to where the horses had been raided.
“Saying, ‘The Chinese raided the horses,’
How can we turn back without attacking the enemy
And show our faces to the people?
In Kakanchin's Beijing,
Even if we are on foot, my foal,
We shall fight until we die!
While this gray head blessed by Khizr remains,
How can we return to the Kyrgyz, saying,
‘We let them be slaughtered on the road’!
Let us turn and enter among the Manchu
And bring splendid slaughter!”
Your prince would rather die for honor
Than fail to go and make war
Upon Kakanchin's Beijing!
He and Khan Bakai together
Took courage, those dear men.
They placed the horseless boys before them
And led them onward;
Lion Bakai led the way,
Taking a direct road toward Beijing.
They crossed rugged ground,
Passed over high, difficult mountain saddles,
And traversed all manner of wondrous places.
Straight-flowing springs and clear water—
He did not wish to stop here.
Uncle Bakai led them onward
Through lands he himself had seen,
Past valleys with springs and streams,
And over rugged open plains—
Taking a direct path across the open plain,
Khan Bakai went
To the ridge of Kara-Kyr,
Along the Üch-Karkyra.
At Kapka-Tash by the Sary-Jaz,
He halted at Kapka-Tash.
His weary heart distressed,
Your dear uncle Bakai
Lamented the days of old!
The reason for his lament was this:
Had Bakai not fought enemies from childhood
And grown accustomed to war?
The marshy ground of Kara-Kyya—
My dear foals,
Yesterday, while lion Manas was alive,
This was where the great host encamped!
Thick with feather grass and without stones,
They called it the Sary-Jaz valley.
If you ask about this place,
It was where horses fattened and grew full;
While lion Manas was alive,
This was where six hundred mares were slaughtered
To feed the army!
Two men shared each portion,
Carving off strips of rich horse-rib fat;
This was a place of abundant delights!
While my thoroughbred Manas was alive,
Horse fat flowed murmuring
Down along the spring!
When we journeyed to Kakan,
This was where the great host
Made merry after wreaking turmoil!
While that Manas was alive,
While our fortune remained whole,
This accursed Bakai did not die
And did not behold judgment!
When the past comes to mind,
My heart is painfully torn;
This accursed, barren world
Seems to have deceived Bakai
As the whim took it!
My heart is grieved, my liver burns;
My companion Manas,
Who knew my inmost secrets, is gone!
Parted from his Manas,
Bakai has not a thread of fortune!
Was it not Bakai who cast
The world behind him?
My dear foals,
Did Bakai not lead the way
To Kakanchin's Beijing
At least seven times?!
Has old age not arrived
And taken up its place beside Bakai?!
Has this accursed, barren world
Not made sport of Bakai
And gone on deceiving him?!
Here he goes on holy war,
And in Khan Bakai's hand
Is the red banner with a golden finial.
When fortune was granted in my youth,
My Kula horse pranced beneath me,
With twelve companions at my side.
Truly, your uncle Bakai
Had Yraman's son Yrchy
Singing beside him,
And my dark diviner Tölö
Casting lots before him.
My jester Chalybai,
Who found the hidden cause of deeds gone astray;
Those unrivaled heroes
Were the generous hero's retinue.
When the Forty Companions traveled in splendor,
My wondrous games and revels—
This accursed, filthy world,
When I look back, never turned its face away!
Grievous hardship comes upon me
When I count the days of old!”
Kökcholok beneath him
Moved as though he might stop,
Rolling across the feather-grass plain,
While Khan Bakai upon him
Shuddered as he told his sorrows!
Your mighty uncle Bakai
Swayed and groaned;
He traveled on grieving,
His old wound stirred anew!
At a divided pass and a white ridge,
Unable to spur onward and cross,
Külchoro and Kanchoro
Could not travel steadily, those two.
The plump, evenly fat youths
Wandered around in circles.
Look here if you would see hardship:
There was no room to take them double,
And when driven on foot, they would not walk.
Refusing to walk, they lingered,
And stopped at the edge of Ak-Chiy.
Unable to contain his anger, roaring,
Your illustrious prince cursed them:
“By God, you two scoundrels,
When I drive you on foot, you will not walk,
And when I take you double, you will not fit.
Nor, you scoundrels, safe and sound,
Would you stay and guard the horses!
You do not heed the words spoken,
And will not go where you are driven!
You do not heed a man's words,
Nor would you remain behind in Talas!
I gathered argamaks, I gathered horses—
May Buurul be accepted in place of those thoroughbreds;
I gathered brave youths, I gathered men—
May Abyke and Köbösh be accepted in place of such kin!
Today I let you block my road to Beijing;
You have made many sorrows boil within me!
You two are left horseless and on foot,
And have brought upon my head
A marvel no one else could achieve!
Can there be men like you?
Is it right to call you men?
Did your hips not ache from lying down?
Was your sleep never sated?
By God, you two scoundrels,
You are no creatures the size of a fist
To be shut inside a saddlebag,
Nor are you small enough to be taken before me,
Nor are you six-year-old children!
By God, you two scoundrels,
Who wandered freely and grew up untended,
Who grew up as equals among the people's sons,
Whose right shoulders grew broad,
Who grew into heroes that shattered the Oirats!
So that your hearts would be rich with courage,
I fed you blood-streaked horse-rib fat;
So that you would become inseparable kin,
I had Kanykei nurse you,
And among the Argyn and Kyrgyz,
When did I ever let anyone call you mere boys!
You two scoundrels did not guard the horses;
This deed of yours is very bad.
When I take you double, you will not fit,
And when I drive you on foot, you will not walk!
You two scoundrels would not find a way
To remain and guard the horses!
You do not understand the words spoken,
And when I drive you, you will not take the road!
You brought hardship upon our reconnaissance
And made us carry your saddles and tack!
You took off your coats upon the steppe;
Parting us from every tulpar,
Boys, you have brought a marvel upon my head.
When we were to reconnoiter the main road,
When we were to drive off
The Chinese people's countless herds,
Even in sleep one would not dream such a dream—
Has any clan ever seen such a deed!
The road to Beijing is exceedingly long;
How shall we set our faces and go?
How shall we now reconnoiter
Fortified Beijing?!
